messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Seventy-year-old Miguel, a widowed Latin American man and retired welder, has been haunted by his traumatic past for years. His experiences of torture have left him with deeply ingrained triggers that repeatedly disrupt his daily life. The sound of gunfire, a sense of entrapment, and any sign of violence can instantly transport him back to the horror he endured. When Miguel encounters these triggers, he often feels as though there are no options for escape or relief. The sound of gunfire, in particular, serves as an intensely distressing reminder of his torture. Recently, while working part-time at a local metal shop, the loud noise from another worker accidentally discharging a pistol sent him into a state of shock and panic. This triggered a series of coping mechanisms he had developed over time. Miguel would detach himself emotionally from the memories, trying to distance himself from the traumatic event. He also became overly compliant whenever he felt threatened, often agreeing with others just to avoid further harm. When Miguel tries to recount what happened during his torture, he struggles to explain clearly and loses track of his thoughts mid-sentence. The memory feels as though it is happening right now rather than something that occurred in the past. This sense of immediacy has made him feel trapped by his experiences. He often finds himself feeling intense rage when he recalls these events. Miguel’s fear that harm can come from anyone and anywhere has significantly impacted how he navigates daily life. The belief that he could have done more to stop what happened, coupled with feelings of self-blame, exacerbates his emotional distress. These negative appraisals lead him to suppress thoughts about the trauma, as they only deepen his sense of guilt and fear. His maladaptive strategies often stem from these negative beliefs. Miguel believes that he can never know who will harm him, which makes it nearly impossible for him to feel safe in any situation. This constant vigilance has led to a series of avoidance behaviors where he tries not to think about the trauma at all. However, this suppression only serves to intensify his triggers and keeps the memory vividly present. The weight of these negative appraisals has become overwhelming, creating a self-reinforcing cycle that Miguel struggles to break. He is certain that if he were more proactive or acted differently during his torture, things would have turned out differently. This belief feeds into his maladaptive strategies, further complicating his ability to process and cope with the trauma. The combination of triggers, memory distortions, negative appraisals, and maladaptive coping mechanisms has led Miguel to a point where he feels trapped in a cycle of fear and guilt that permeates every aspect of his life. His attempts to avoid these painful memories have only made them more potent, as he finds himself constantly reacting to reminders and triggers. Miguel finally decided to seek help after an incident at work triggered a particularly severe episode. He realized that he could no longer continue living in fear and wanted support to break this cycle. What frightened him most was the prospect of never finding peace or understanding from his experiences, but what he hoped for was a chance to reclaim his life and find some form of healing.
